headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 5 studies yielded an effect size of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.6–1.04), indicating no statistically significant association between Vitamin E and bladder cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 57.93%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.

effect_size.excerpt: In quartile analysis, using subjects with the lowest alpha-tocopherol level as the reference group, the adjusted ORs and 95% CIs for the second, third, and fourth quartiles were 0.75 (0.50-1.14), 0.69 (0.46-1.05), and 0.50 (0.32-0.78), respectively (P for trend = 0.003). Increased retinol level was also associated with reduced risk with OR of 0.57 (95% CI: 0.40-0.81).

sample_size.excerpt: Source documentation was obtained on 229 cases. Upon review 3 patients were excluded from analysis because they were misreported as bladder cancer, and 2 were excluded due to insufficient source documentation to confirm the diagnosis, leaving 224 bladder cancer among the 34,887 eligible, evaluable SELECT participants.( 18 ) Of the 35,533 men who were randomized 646 were excluded from all analyses, including 10 due to prior diagnosis of prostate cancer (in another the diagnosis was discovered after primary publication) and 15 who never received proper informed consent, while all 621 participants from 2 clinical sites were excluded due to severe data and participant management problems.

cases.excerpt: Table 1 lists the characteristics of the 224 men with and the 34,663 without bladder cancer.
